questions.stem: How does 8.03 direct the crew to confirm the pleural space has been entered before the tube is inserted?
options: Insert a gloved finger and hook it to touch the inner side of the ribs
Attach the Heimlich valve and look for fluctuation
Listen for a rush of air as the Kelly clamp is withdrawn
Advance the tube until the depth marking exceeds 6 cm
questions.explanation: Hooking a finger onto the inner surface of the ribs proves the track is intrapleural rather than in a subcutaneous or extrapleural plane. 8.03 warns that rib fractures may be present and can lacerate the finger.

questions.stem: In which direction does 8.03 direct the chest tube to be advanced?
questions.explanation: 8.03 directs the tube cephalad and posterior until all the holes are inside the chest. In a supine patient air collects apically and blood posteriorly, so this track drains both.

questions.stem: What minimum chest tube depth marking does 8.03 expect once the tube is in place?
questions.explanation: A depth marking greater than 6 cm at the skin tells the crew the fenestrated portion of the tube has cleared the chest wall. A shallower reading suggests a side hole is sitting in soft tissue, which will leak air subcutaneously.

questions.stem: What does 8.03 identify as signs of proper chest tube placement and patency after the Heimlich valve is attached?
options: Continuous bubbling in the valve chamber
Absence of breath sounds on the treated side
Fluctuation of the valve with ventilation and improved compliance
A sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: 8.03 uses valve fluctuation with each breath plus improvement in compliance or respiratory status as the bedside evidence the tube is in the pleural space and open. A static valve suggests an obstructed or malpositioned tube.

questions.stem: At what chest tube output does 8.03 direct the crew to clamp the tube to avoid exsanguination?
options: > 1000 mL of blood in less than 60 minutes
> 500 mL of blood in less than 30 minutes
> 1000 mL of blood in less than 15 minutes
> 1500 mL of blood in less than 60 minutes
questions.explanation: Output above 1000 mL in under an hour means the tube is draining a patient faster than they can be transfused, so 8.03 clamps it deliberately to let the hemothorax tamponade the bleeding.

questions.stem: After clamping a chest tube for high output, what does 8.03 direct the crew to monitor for?
options: An air leak at the insertion site
questions.explanation: Clamping trades drainage for tamponade, so the pleural collection can re-accumulate under tension. 8.03 also has the crew notify the receiving facility of the output and the clamped tube, since the patient likely needs emergent OR.

questions.stem: What does 8.03 require to be documented before a chest tube procedure is finalized in the chart?
options: The time the Heimlich valve was attached
The depth marking and the size of the tube used
The total volume of lidocaine infiltrated
The name of the receiving physician who verified placement
questions.explanation: 8.03 forbids documenting the procedure as 'successful' without naming the physician who verified placement. If the crew is later told placement was incorrect, they must notify the Clinical Manager on Call and complete a QM report.

questions.stem: What quick method does 8.03 give for assessing the chest tube incision site?
options: Measuring four finger-breadths below the clavicle
Counting down from the sternal angle
The handshake in the axilla method
questions.explanation: 8.03 adopted the handshake-in-the-axilla method because the previous wording — lateral to the superior aspect of the inframammary crease — led providers to place tubes inferiorly, since the crease projects higher than most people expect.

questions.stem: Which rhythms does 8.04 list as indications for defibrillation?
options: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Any wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse
Refractory VF after three shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone
questions.explanation: 8.04 limits defibrillation to VF and pulseless VT; any rhythm with a pulse, PEA and asystole are explicit contraindications. Refractory VF after three shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone is the indication for 8.05 Dual Sequential External Defibrillation.

questions.stem: What does 8.04 give as contraindications to defibrillation?
options: Any rhythm with a pulse, PEA and asystole
questions.explanation: Shocking a perfusing rhythm can induce VF, and neither PEA nor asystole is a shockable rhythm, so 8.04 rules out all three. Chest hair is a pad-adhesion problem to be clipped or shaved, not a reason to withhold the shock.

questions.stem: What therapy electrode placement does 8.04 give as preferred?
questions.explanation: 8.04 names AP as the preferred placement, and also requires that the therapy electrodes make good skin contact and do not cover any part of the ECG electrodes.

questions.stem: What does 8.04 direct for a patient with excessive chest hair before therapy pads are applied?
options: Apply conductive gel over the hair
Press the pads firmly without clipping
questions.explanation: Hair holds the pad off the skin, and the resulting air gap is what produces arcing and burns. 8.04 has the crew remove clothing, dry the chest and clip or shave excess hair so the electrodes adhere.

questions.stem: What happens if the selected energy is changed while the defibrillator is charging or charged, per 8.04?
options: The unit locks out until the pads are replaced
The unit delivers the previously selected energy
The unit disarms itself and must be recharged
The unit charges to the new level automatically
questions.explanation: Changing energy mid-charge disarms the unit, so the crew must press CHARGE again to charge to the new level. A crew that does not know this can stand clear expecting a shock that will never be delivered.

questions.stem: What does 8.04 say about how the SHOCK button must be operated?
options: Hold it down for a full five seconds
Press and hold until energy is delivered
questions.explanation: 8.04 requires pressing and holding the SHOCK button on the front panel until the energy is actually delivered; a quick tap may not discharge the unit. Pressing the Disarm softkey cancels the shock at any point.

questions.stem: What complication does 8.04 attribute to poor pad adherence or air trapped under the therapy electrodes?
options: Delivery of a double dose of energy
questions.explanation: 8.04 directs the crew to apply one edge of the pad and roll it smoothly to the other so no air pockets are trapped between gel and skin. Trapped air lets current arc, which burns the patient and wastes delivered energy.

questions.stem: What does 8.05 require before Dual Sequential External Defibrillation is used?
options: Asystole persisting through two rounds of epinephrine
Refractory VF after two shocks and one dose of epinephrine
Any pulseless rhythm not responding to five minutes of CPR
Refractory VF or pulseless VT despite three shocks, epinephrine and amiodarone
questions.explanation: DSED is a rescue for VF or pulseless VT that has already failed three defibrillations, epinephrine and amiodarone. Like single-shock defibrillation, it is contraindicated for any rhythm with a pulse, PEA and asystole.

questions.stem: How does 8.05 direct the second set of defibrillation pads to be placed?
options: Anterior-posterior if the first set is anterior-lateral
Anterior-lateral regardless of the first set's position
Directly over the first set for maximum vector overlap
Both sets anterior-lateral on opposite sides of the chest
questions.explanation: 8.05 alternates the vectors — anterior-posterior if the first set is anterior-lateral and vice versa — and insists there be no overlap or contact between the two sets. The second set goes on with minimal interruption to CPR.

questions.stem: What does 8.05 warn is the risk if the two sets of defibrillation pads overlap or touch?
options: Arcing and skin burns on the patient
Significant risk of damaging the defibrillators
Delivery of only one of the two shocks
Failure of the second monitor to charge
questions.explanation: Current from one unit can be driven back into the other through contacting pads, which is why 8.05 requires separation and opposing vectors. Losing both defibrillators mid-arrest ends the resuscitation.

questions.stem: Who operates the defibrillators during Dual Sequential External Defibrillation under 8.05?
options: The provider managing the airway operates both
The crew member performing CPR operates both
questions.explanation: 8.05 has a single provider run both units so the shocks land as close together as possible but not simultaneously. Two operators cannot reliably achieve that sub-second separation.

questions.stem: How far apart does 8.05 say the two DSED shocks should ideally be delivered?
questions.explanation: 8.05 wants the shocks as close together as possible but explicitly not at the same time, ideally under one second apart — hence 'shock one' called aloud as it is delivered, then immediately 'shock two'.

questions.stem: At what point in the DSED sequence does 8.05 direct both defibrillators to be charged?
options: After the pulse and rhythm check
After confirming refractory VF on both monitors
Immediately after the second set of pads is placed
questions.explanation: Charging both units to the maximum setting during compressions keeps the hands-off interval short: CPR stops only once both are charged, for a pulse and rhythm check and to confirm refractory V-Fib/V-Tach on both monitors.

questions.stem: How many filters does 8.06 require for an epoprostenol transport, and where do they go?
options: Three: one on the inspiratory limb, two on the expiratory limb
Three: two on the inspiratory limb, one on the expiratory limb
One HMEF on the inspiratory limb only
Two: one on each limb of the ventilator circuit
questions.explanation: 8.06 uses three filters — one for the inhalation port and two for exhalation — with the inspiratory filter placed closest to the Hamilton. They must be filters from the sending hospital, not the HMEFs normally used on the circuit.

questions.stem: Where on the ventilator circuit does 8.06 place the Aerogen delivering epoprostenol?
options: At the patient wye, before the HMEF
In line with the exhalation valve
On the inspiratory limb, after the filter
On the expiratory limb, after the filters
questions.explanation: The nebulizer must sit downstream of the inspiratory filter so the aerosol reaches the patient rather than being trapped, while the two expiratory filters protect the ventilator and the cabin from exhaled drug.

questions.stem: What are the typical inhaled epoprostenol doses 8.06 tells a crew to expect?
questions.explanation: 8.06 has the crew verify the running dose with the sending provider; typical doses are 10 – 50 nanograms/kg/minute. Confusing nanograms with micrograms would be a thousand-fold error.

questions.stem: On which body weight does 8.06 say inhaled epoprostenol is dosed?
questions.explanation: 8.06 has the crew confirm with the sending provider both the dose and that it is being calculated on ideal body weight — a check worth making, because an obese patient dosed on actual weight would be receiving substantially more drug.

questions.stem: What battery life does 8.06 give for a fully charged Aerogen Pro-X controller?
questions.explanation: The Pro-X holds up to 45 minutes of charge but must be plugged in to run continuously; unplugged it drops to 30-minute mode. The USB controller has no battery at all and must stay powered from the Hamilton T-1 or a wall outlet.

questions.stem: When does 8.06 direct the crew to unplug the Aerogen controller at the sending facility?
options: Just prior to leaving the bedside
Only if the Pro-X battery is fully charged
Before switching the patient to the LFN ventilator
After the patient is loaded in the aircraft
questions.explanation: Unplugging last keeps the Pro-X out of its 30-minute mode for as long as possible. Once in the ambulance or aircraft it is plugged back in and AC power confirmed, along with the syringe pump and the Hamilton.

questions.stem: What does 8.06 say about titrating inhaled epoprostenol during transport?
options: It is titrated to the PA pressure
It is titrated to an SpO2 above 93%
It is not titrated without a physician's order
It is weaned over the final 10 minutes of transport
questions.explanation: 8.06 states the crew does not titrate this medication without an order from a physician. The crew's role is to monitor PA pressures if a catheter is present and report changes to the receiving facility, not to adjust the rate.

questions.stem: What does 8.06 direct the crew to monitor during transport if a PA catheter is present?
options: Wedge pressure before and after takeoff
PA pressures, reporting changes to the receiving
questions.explanation: Inhaled epoprostenol is given to drop pulmonary vascular resistance, so the PA pressure is the direct measure of whether it is still working — and a rise is the first sign that delivery has been interrupted.

questions.stem: Why does 8.06 state that inhaled epoprostenol cannot be stopped during transport?
options: The syringe pump cannot be restarted in flight
It causes rebound bronchospasm on withdrawal
It has an extremely short half-life
The Aerogen cup cannot be refilled once empty
questions.explanation: The extremely short half-life means pulmonary vasodilation is lost within minutes of any interruption, with rebound pulmonary hypertension. That is also why 8.06 asks for a backup syringe of epoprostenol when one is available.

questions.stem: What does 8.06 require of the Aerogen solo cup throughout transport?
options: It must be kept below the patient's airway
It must be disconnected during ascent
It must be refilled every hour
questions.explanation: The vibrating mesh aperture plate only nebulizes drug sitting against it, so tipping the solo cup interrupts delivery of a medication that cannot be stopped. 8.06 pairs this with keeping the syringe pump free of alarms.

questions.stem: Which situation does 8.07 list as an indication for endotracheal tube exchange?
options: A damaged or uncuffed ETT causing a significant air leak
ETT migration correctable by repositioning the tube
A tube that has become difficult to suction
Inadequate cuff inflation correctable by adding air
questions.explanation: 8.07 reserves exchange for a damaged or uncuffed tube with a significant air leak, or a tube depth that is wrong and is causing ventilation or oxygenation failure. Problems fixable by repositioning or by inflating the cuff further are contraindications.

questions.stem: Which situation does 8.07 list as a contraindication to endotracheal tube exchange?
options: A tube depth causing oxygenation failure
A damaged pilot balloon on the cuff
ETT migration correctable by less invasive means
An uncuffed ETT with a significant air leak
questions.explanation: Exchange risks injury or loss of the airway, so 8.07 rules it out whenever a less invasive fix exists — repositioning a migrated tube, or simply adding air to an underinflated cuff.

questions.stem: What equipment does 8.07 list for an endotracheal tube exchange?
options: An airway exchange catheter with an oxygen adapter
A supraglottic airway and a video laryngoscope only
A tube exchanger catheter and a fiberoptic scope
Everything required for intubation, plus a bougie
questions.explanation: 8.07 treats the exchange as an intubation that happens to start with a tube already in place, so the full intubation setup must be ready — plus a bougie, which is the device that holds the tracheal path between the two tubes.

questions.stem: How does 8.07 direct pre-oxygenation before an endotracheal tube exchange?
options: Hyperventilate to an end-tidal CO2 below 30
Increase PEEP to 10 and place a nasal cannula at 6 LPM
Increase FiO2 to 100% and place a nasal cannula at 15 LPM
Increase FiO2 to 100% and give three minutes of BVM
questions.explanation: The apnoeic period during an exchange is the dangerous part, so 8.07 denitrogenates on 100% FiO2 and adds a nasal cannula at 15 LPM for apnoeic oxygenation while the tube is out. Additional sedation and paralysis are given as for RSI.

questions.stem: How far does 8.07 direct the bougie to be advanced through the existing endotracheal tube?
options: Until 10 cm has passed beyond the tube tip
To the depth of the original tube's 23 cm mark
Until resistance is felt at the carina
To the markings indicating mid-trachea, no deeper
questions.explanation: The assistant advances the bougie gently to the markings indicating mid-trachea and stops if hold-up is encountered. Going deeper risks airway trauma or pneumothorax, and 8.07 requires the bougie to stay at that depth for the whole procedure.

questions.stem: In 8.07, what does the crew do immediately before the old endotracheal tube is withdrawn?
questions.explanation: The cuff is deflated only after laryngoscopy has established and is maintaining a view of the glottic opening, so if the tube comes out early the operator can still see the cords and the bougie passing through them.

questions.stem: Once the old ETT tip clears the mouth during an exchange under 8.07, who controls the bougie?
options: Neither — the bougie is released to prevent torque
The operator takes and maintains control of the bougie
Control alternates with each centimeter withdrawn
The assistant keeps control of the bougie throughout
questions.explanation: 8.07 hands control of the bougie back and forth deliberately: the assistant holds it while the operator withdraws the old tube, the operator takes it once the tip is clear so the assistant can strip the tube off, then the assistant retakes it as the new tube is advanced. The bougie is never unheld.

questions.stem: What manoeuvre does 8.07 use as the new tube is advanced over the bougie, and why?
options: A BURP manoeuvre to align the glottic opening
A jaw thrust to lift the epiglottis off the tube
A 90-degree counter-clockwise turn to clear the arytenoid cartilage
A 90-degree clockwise turn to open the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Rotating the tube 90 degrees counter-clockwise turns the bevel away from the right arytenoid, which is where a tube railroaded over a bougie typically hangs up. The laryngoscopic view is maintained throughout the advance.

questions.stem: What does 8.07 give as the final steps once the new tube is in the trachea?
options: Verify placement, remove the laryngoscope, then inflate the cuff
Inflate the cuff, remove the bougie, verify placement, secure the tube
Secure the tube, then inflate the cuff and remove the bougie
Remove the bougie, obtain a chest x-ray, then inflate the cuff
questions.explanation: 8.07 inflates the cuff before the bougie comes out so ventilation can begin immediately, then verifies placement and secures the tube. Securing before confirming would commit the crew to an unverified airway.

questions.stem: What does 8.07 state about performing an endotracheal tube exchange blind?
options: It must never be done blind
It is preferred when the laryngoscopic view is poor
It is acceptable with a bougie in place
It is acceptable if the original airway was easy
questions.explanation: 8.07 requires visualization of the glottic opening throughout and says the procedure must NEVER be performed blind. Keeping it as close as possible to a standard intubation means the crew's usual rescue principles still apply if it goes wrong.

questions.stem: Which single finding must be present before a finger thoracostomy may be performed under 8.08?
questions.explanation: 8.08 states in red that hypotension is REQUIRED to perform a finger thoracostomy. Tachycardia, JVD and tracheal deviation are supporting signs of peri-arrest tension physiology, but none of them substitutes for hypotension as the trigger to cut.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a contraindication to finger thoracostomy in 8.08?
questions.explanation: Simple pneumothorax, normotension and hypertension are the listed contraindications — without tension physiology and hypotension there is nothing to decompress. Traumatic arrest is itself an indication, and decreased breath sounds and falling ETCO2 are supporting signs of tension.

questions.stem: Where does 8.08 place the incision for a finger thoracostomy?
options: 4th or 5th intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary lines
2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
4th or 5th intercostal space at the posterior axillary line
questions.explanation: The incision is lateral to the nipple at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary lines. The 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line is a needle thoracostomy site, not a finger thoracostomy site.

questions.stem: If the provider is in doubt about which rib interspace to use for a finger thoracostomy, what does 8.08 advise?
options: Err one rib interspace more superior
Err one rib interspace more inferior
Default to the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
Confirm the interspace with ultrasound before cutting
questions.explanation: 8.08 directs erring one interspace more superior when in doubt. Going too low risks entering the abdomen through the diaphragm, which is a far worse error than opening the chest one space high.

questions.stem: Which instrument does 8.08 use to pass through the soft tissue and enter the pleural space after the skin incision?
questions.explanation: The #10 scalpel makes the skin incision only; the large Kelly clamp, held by the shanks, is pushed through the soft tissue to the rib and then over its superior border into the pleural space. The Ruiz hook and bougie belong to the surgical cricothyrotomy kit.

questions.stem: Which structures does 8.08 warn lie at the inferior border of the rib and must be avoided during a finger thoracostomy?
options: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve
questions.explanation: The neurovascular bundle runs in the groove along the inferior rib border, so the clamp is pressed over the TOP of the rib. Striking that bundle causes brisk arterial bleeding into a chest that is already compromised.

questions.stem: In 8.08, what is the next step immediately after the Kelly clamp has been pressed over the rib and into the pleural space?
options: Spread the clamp as you pull it out to enlarge the opening
Insert a gloved finger to verify entry into the pleura
Place a vented chest seal over the site
questions.explanation: The opening is enlarged by spreading the Kelly clamp as it is withdrawn, and only then is the gloved finger inserted to verify the pleura has been entered. Inserting the finger into an unspread tract usually fails to confirm anything.

questions.stem: How does 8.08 direct the crew to verify that the pleural space has actually been entered?
options: Insert a gloved finger and hook it against the inner side of the ribs
Auscultate for returning breath sounds on the treated side
Observe a rise in ETCO2 on the waveform
Look for a rush of air escaping the incision
questions.explanation: Confirmation is tactile: a gloved finger is inserted and hooked to feel the inner surface of the ribs. 8.08 also warns that rib fractures may be present and can lacerate the finger.

questions.stem: What estimated volume of blood return from a finger thoracostomy prompts an occlusive dressing and initiation of blood products?
questions.explanation: Excessive blood return estimated at more than 1000 mL means the open chest is now the exsanguination route, so the site is occluded deliberately to tamponade and blood products are started. The crew must then watch for a recurrent tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: The patient re-tensions after a finger thoracostomy. What does 8.08 direct the crew to do?
options: Insert a finger into the existing incision
Make a new incision one interspace more superior
Perform a needle decompression on the same side
Place a vented chest seal over the incision
questions.explanation: The tract is already there; re-tensioning means it has sealed over, so the finger goes back into the existing incision to re-open the pleura. A second incision or a needle adds injury without addressing the closed tract.

questions.stem: Which patient presentation is listed as an indication for the Flow-Safe II CPAP delivery system?
questions.explanation: CHF/pulmonary edema, asthma/COPD, moderate to severe respiratory distress and pre-oxygenation for RSI are the indications. Pneumothorax, frank respiratory failure and severe altered LOC are all contraindications — CPAP needs a patient who can breathe and protect the airway.

questions.stem: Below what systolic blood pressure is the Flow-Safe II CPAP system contraindicated?
questions.explanation: 8.09 lists SBP < 100 as a contraindication. Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return, so CPAP can tip a marginally compensated patient into frank hypotension.

questions.stem: At or below what weight are pediatric patients contraindicated for the Flow-Safe II CPAP system, absent a ventilator malfunction?
questions.explanation: Pediatric patients weighing 15 kg or less are a contraindication unless the ventilator has malfunctioned. The Flow-Safe II is a fixed, flow-driven device with no ability to scale safely to a small child.

questions.stem: On the Flow-Safe II flow chart, which oxygen flow rate corresponds to a desired PEEP of 10 cmH2O?
questions.explanation: The chart attached to the oxygen tubing pairs 5 cmH2O with 8–9 LPM, 7.5 cmH2O with 10–12 LPM, 10 cmH2O with 13–14 LPM, and 13 cmH2O (the maximum) with flush. The Flow-Safe II has no PEEP dial — flow IS the PEEP setting.

questions.stem: By how much may the pressure shown on the Flow-Safe II manometer differ from the desired CPAP level, per 8.09?
questions.explanation: 8.09 accepts a reading within ± 3 cmH2O of the desired CPAP. A larger discrepancy usually means a mask leak, which is corrected by repositioning or changing mask size rather than by turning up the flow.

questions.stem: A patient requires both ventilatory and oxygenation support. What does 8.09 direct instead of the Flow-Safe II?
options: CPAP at a higher PEEP level
questions.explanation: The Flow-Safe II provides CPAP only, so it supports oxygenation but does nothing for ventilation. A patient who is also failing to ventilate needs BiPAP delivered through the transport ventilator.

questions.stem: If nebulized medication is needed for a patient on the Flow-Safe II, where does 8.09 direct the nebulizer to be connected?
options: Between the mask and the Flow-Safe manometer via a T piece
Between the flow sensor and the ETT
Upstream of the device at the oxygen source
questions.explanation: The nebulizer set-up goes between the mask and the manometer using a T piece, so the drug is delivered close to the patient without disturbing the pressure reading. Its own oxygen tubing must run to a secondary oxygen source.

questions.stem: When a nebulizer is added to the Flow-Safe II circuit, where does 8.09 direct its oxygen tubing to be connected?
options: To the same oxygen source driving the CPAP
To a flow meter Christmas tree on the CPAP line
questions.explanation: The nebulizer runs off a second oxygen source. Sharing the CPAP source would steal flow and drop the delivered PEEP, which on this device is set purely by flow rate.

questions.stem: Which patient condition is listed as an indication for gastric tube insertion in 8.10?
questions.explanation: Intubation, comatose patients, GI bleeds, overdoses, gastric distension and gastric obstruction are the indications. Esophageal rupture, caustic ingestion and severe facial trauma are contraindications — in each, blind tube passage risks creating or extending a perforation.

questions.stem: A patient who needs gastric decompression has had recent nasal surgery. What does 8.10 direct?
options: Place a nasogastric tube in the opposite nare
Place the nasogastric tube with extra lubrication
questions.explanation: Recent nasal surgery is a contraindication to the nasal route only — 8.10 specifically notes an OG may be placed. The other listed contraindications (esophageal rupture, caustic ingestion) rule out both routes.

questions.stem: How does 8.10 direct nasogastric tube insertion depth to be measured?
options: Tip of the nose to the corner of the ear, then to the xiphoid process
Corner of the mouth to the tip of the ear, then to the xiphoid process
Tip of the nose to the earlobe, then to the umbilicus
Corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, then to the sternal notch
questions.explanation: The NG measurement starts at the tip of the nose; the mouth-to-ear-to-xiphoid route is the orogastric measurement. Using the OG measurement for an NG leaves the tube short of the stomach by roughly the length of the nasal passage.

questions.stem: During nasogastric tube insertion the patient begins to cough and develops new onset dyspnea. What does 8.10 direct?
options: Withdraw the tube slightly and reassess
Continue advancing as the patient swallows
questions.explanation: Coughing or new dyspnea suggests the tube has entered the airway, so 8.10 directs removal rather than repositioning. Continuing to advance risks intubating the trachea with a gastric tube.

questions.stem: What size syringe does 8.10 specify for aspirating gastric contents to assess tube placement?
questions.explanation: A 60 mL syringe is connected and aspirated back while assessing for gastric contents. The same assessment then uses a separate injection of air while listening over the stomach.

questions.stem: After aspirating for gastric contents, how much air does 8.10 direct to be injected while listening over the stomach?
questions.explanation: Roughly 20 mL of air is injected and the crew listens or feels for the air rush in the stomach. This applies identically to the nasogastric and orogastric routes.

questions.stem: Once gastric tube placement is confirmed, what does 8.10 specify about securing the tube?
options: Tape it in place, but not to the ETT
Tape it to the ETT so the two move together
Suture it in place before transport
Secure it with a commercial tube holder
questions.explanation: 8.10 explicitly states the gastric tube should NOT be taped to the ETT. Tying the two together means any tug on the gastric tube transmits directly to the airway and risks extubation.

questions.stem: Before packing a hemostatic agent into a wound, what does 8.11 direct be done first?
options: Remove any saturated gauze from the wound
Irrigate the wound with sterile saline
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
Pack the wound with plain gauze first
questions.explanation: Saturated gauze is removed so the hemostatic agent can make direct contact with the bleeding vessels. An agent packed on top of blood-soaked gauze never reaches the source and will fail.

questions.stem: After packing rolled gauze into the wound, how long does 8.11 direct direct pressure to be held?
questions.explanation: 8.11 directs a continuous 3 minutes of direct pressure on the bleeding source through the packed gauze. Releasing early is the most common reason a hemostatic dressing fails.

questions.stem: A hemostatic dressing packed into a wound is now fully red. What does 8.11 direct?
options: Remove it and replace it with a new hemostatic dressing
Add a second dressing on top and hold pressure
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
Wrap and tie the bandage to maintain pressure
questions.explanation: A fully red dressing means the agent was not applied to the bleeding source or pressure was not held long enough, so it is removed and replaced rather than layered over. Wrapping and tying is only done once bleeding is actually controlled.

questions.stem: With which agent are QuickClot dressings impregnated, per 8.11 PEARLS?
questions.explanation: QuickClot uses kaolin, an inorganic mineral. 8.11 specifically notes the dressings contain no human, animal or shellfish product and do not cause an exothermic reaction, so shellfish allergy and burn risk are not reasons to withhold them.

questions.stem: How long may a hemostatic dressing remain in a wound, per 8.11 PEARLS?
questions.explanation: Dressings can stay packed for up to 24 hours, which comfortably covers any transport. There is no reason to disturb a controlled wound en route — 8.11 warns 'if you peek, you leak.'

questions.stem: Besides major hemorrhage, what other use for hemostatic agents does 8.11 PEARLS describe?
options: Controlling nuisance bleeding such as head lacerations
Control of epistaxis after nasal airway placement
questions.explanation: 8.11 notes hemostatic agents are not reserved for exsanguinating injury — they are effective for persistent 'nuisance bleeding' such as scalp lacerations that would otherwise consume crew attention throughout transport.

questions.stem: A patient is being prepared for RSI. What role does 8.12 give to high flow nasal cannula?
options: Pre-oxygenation and apneic oxygenation during RSI
A bridge to CPAP after extubation
questions.explanation: Pre and apneic oxygenation during RSI is an explicit indication — the high flow continues to drive oxygen into the airway through the apneic period. Hypoxia, hypercarbia and mild to moderate respiratory distress are the other listed indications.

questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates high flow nasal cannula under 8.12?
questions.explanation: Basilar skull fracture is a contraindication because high flow into the nasopharynx can be driven through the skull base defect. Hypoxia, hypercarbia and mild to moderate distress are indications for the therapy.

questions.stem: What adult flow rate range does 8.12 give for high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Adults are run at 8–60 LPM, titrated to work of breathing while FiO2 is titrated to oxygenation. The weight-based 0.5–1 L/kg/min figure is the pediatric rate, and the single-digit LPM figures belong to the Flow-Safe II CPAP chart.

questions.stem: What pediatric flow rate range does 8.12 give for high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: Pediatric HFNC starts at 0.5–1 L/kg/min. The 2 L/kg/min and 20 LPM figures are the ceiling that may be used only when transporting without heat and humidification, not the starting range.

questions.stem: To what may the pediatric HFNC flow be titrated if there is no heat or humidification, per 8.12?
questions.explanation: Without heat and humidification the pediatric flow may be titrated up to 2 L/kg/min or 20 LPM. The 60 LPM ceiling applies to adults only.

questions.stem: What does 8.12 require before transporting an adult on HFNC without heat and/or humidification?
options: Approval from the sending provider or OLMC
A physician escort for the transport
Notification of the receiving facility only
questions.explanation: 8.12 carries this in a red box: approval from the sending provider or OLMC is required for unheated, unhumidified HFNC in adults, because dry high flow gas rapidly dries secretions and injures the nasal mucosa.

questions.stem: How does 8.12 direct the RAM cannula prongs to be sized against the patient's nares?
options: They should not occlude more than 80% of the nares
They should completely occlude the nares to hold pressure
They should occlude roughly half of the nares
They should be sized to the smaller of the two nares
questions.explanation: The prongs must leave a leak — no more than 80% occlusion — so that exhaled gas can escape. A fully occlusive fit converts HFNC into an uncontrolled positive-pressure device.

questions.stem: Which Hamilton T-1 mode does 8.12 direct for delivering high flow nasal cannula?
questions.explanation: HFNC is run in HiFloO2 mode found under Noninvasive, with FiO2 and flow set independently. LPO is not available at all while HiFloO2 is running.

questions.stem: A patient on high flow nasal cannula deteriorates during transport. What does 8.12 direct the crew to consider?
options: Increasing the flow rate above 60 LPM
Adding LPO mode to conserve oxygen
questions.explanation: HFNC has a ceiling; a deteriorating patient escalates to CPAP, BiPAP or RSI rather than to more flow. LPO is unavailable during HFNC therapy and a non-rebreather is a step down, not up.

questions.stem: Which oxygen-conserving ventilator mode is unavailable while HFNC therapy is running, per 8.12 PEARLS?
questions.explanation: LPO cannot be used during HFNC. If oxygen conservation becomes necessary on a long transport, 8.12 directs switching the patient to CPAP or BiPAP instead — which is why the LFN oxygen calculator must be run before departure.

questions.stem: What does 8.12 PEARLS give as the therapeutic goal of high flow oxygen therapy?
options: Increase PaO2 to widen the oxygen diffusion gradient
Generate a set level of positive end-expiratory pressure
Unload the diaphragm to reduce work of breathing
Provide ventilatory as well as oxygenation support
questions.explanation: High flow delivers volumes beyond what the patient ventilates, washing out CO2 from the upper airway and raising delivered O2; the stated goal is a higher PaO2 and therefore a steeper diffusion gradient. It is not a pressure-targeted mode.

questions.stem: If a Hamilton T-1 is not readily available, what alternative does 8.12 PEARLS permit for the RAM cannula?
options: Regular oxygen tubing on a flow meter Christmas tree
A Flow-Safe II CPAP device with the mask removed
An LTV ventilator run in HiFloO2 mode
A non-rebreather reservoir line at 15 LPM
questions.explanation: The RAM cannula can be driven from regular oxygen tubing on a standard flow meter, but 8.12 warns this gives a reduced maximum flow rate and no humidification.

questions.stem: How many autofill cycles does the internal helium reservoir of the Maquet IABP hold?
questions.explanation: The internal reservoir carries enough helium for 36 autofill cycles. Because altitude change, power cycling and run time all consume cycles, the crew must budget them against the planned flight profile.

questions.stem: How many autofill cycles does the Maquet IABP perform each time the pump is powered on or off, or the balloon is disconnected and reconnected?
questions.explanation: Each power cycle or balloon disconnect/reconnect costs 6 autofill cycles out of a reservoir of 36. Needless power cycling on the ramp can consume a third of the available helium before the flight begins.

questions.stem: During IABP transport, at what interval of altitude GAIN does the Maquet pump perform an autofill cycle?
questions.explanation: An internal transducer senses barometric change, triggering one autofill for every 1000 feet of climb and one for every 2000 feet of descent. Climbing therefore burns helium twice as fast as descending.

questions.stem: Apart from altitude change, at what interval does the Maquet IABP perform an additional autofill cycle?
questions.explanation: One extra autofill occurs for every 2 hours of pump operation. On a long fixed-wing leg this time-based consumption must be added to the altitude-driven cycles when estimating remaining helium.

questions.stem: To what pressure does 8.13 direct the IABP flush bag pressure infuser to be inflated?
questions.explanation: The pressure bag is inflated to 300 mmHg, the line flushed for several seconds, and the zero button held for two seconds. Too little pressure allows blood to track back and damp or clot the inner lumen.

questions.stem: The patient arrives on an Arrow pump with an Arrow fiber-optic balloon. What does 8.13 require when transferring to the Maquet console?
options: Use the pressure cable and transducer for the IAB
Zero the fiber-optic cable before pressing START
Connect the fiber-optic sensor cable first
Run the pump in semi-auto mode for the transport
questions.explanation: An Arrow fiber-optic balloon will not communicate with the Maquet console, so timing must come from the conventional pressure cable and transducer. Connecting the fiber-optic cable first applies only to a Maquet/Datascope balloon.

questions.stem: The IABP arterial pressure waveform becomes damped in flight. What does 8.13 direct first?
options: Aspirate 3 mL from the IAB inner lumen and discard it
Flush the inner lumen for 15 seconds
Place the pump on standby and switch to semi-auto
Cap the lumen and use an alternative pressure source
questions.explanation: Aspirating 3 mL first tells you whether the lumen is patent. If blood returns, the line is flushed for 15 seconds with the pump on standby; if nothing aspirates, the lumen is presumed clotted and is capped with an alternative pressure source used.

questions.stem: How often does 8.13 direct the IAB inner lumen to be flushed during transport to prevent damping?
questions.explanation: A brief flush of the inner lumen every 15 minutes maintains patency. Losing the pressure waveform in flight costs the trigger source for timing if no fiber-optic cable is in place.

questions.stem: Where should the IABP Augmentation alarm be set relative to the patient's augmented diastolic pressure?
questions.explanation: The augmentation alarm is set 10 mmHg below the patient's augmented diastolic pressure, roughly 3 minutes after assist begins. Set that close, any real loss of augmentation alarms promptly instead of being missed.

questions.stem: Which operation mode does 8.13 designate as the default on the Maquet IABP?
questions.explanation: Auto is the default; semi-auto is rarely needed. In auto the pump selects the lead and trigger and manages inflation/deflation timing continuously, which is what you want in a vibrating, noisy aircraft.

questions.stem: After the IABP and patient are loaded into the rotor-wing aircraft, where does 8.13 direct the pump to be secured?
options: Between the stretcher and the aft-facing seat
Behind the forward-facing seat, left of the loading door
On the brownline rail with the foam pad removed
At the forward bulkhead beside the patient's head
questions.explanation: In the rotor the IABP sits between the stretcher and the aft-facing seat; behind the forward-facing seat left of the patient loading door is the fixed-wing position. In both, the foam pad keeps the pump off the brownline rail and Pilatus tie-down straps run through the pump handles.

questions.stem: Which airway reflex finding does 8.14 require before an i-gel is placed?
questions.explanation: The indication is an unconscious patient with respiratory compromise AND an absent gag reflex; a responsive patient with a gag reflex is an explicit contraindication, since the device will be rejected or provoke vomiting.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as a contraindication to the i-gel in 8.14?
questions.explanation: Known esophageal disease, caustic ingestion and a responsive patient with a gag reflex are the contraindications. Unconsciousness, respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex together form the indication.

questions.stem: Using the 8.14 sizing table, which i-gel size is indicated for a 70 kg adult?
questions.explanation: Size 4 (green) is the medium adult device covering 50–90 kg. Size 3 is the small adult at 30–60 kg and size 5 the large adult at 90+ kg, so a 70 kg patient falls squarely in size 4.

questions.stem: What type of lubricant does 8.14 specify for the i-gel?
questions.explanation: A small bolus of water-based lubricant is used on the back, sides and front of the cuff; 8.14 explicitly prohibits silicone-based lubricants. No bolus may be left sitting in the bowl of the cuff, where it would be driven into the airway on insertion.

questions.stem: In which position does 8.14 direct the patient's head and neck for i-gel insertion, trauma permitting?
options: Sniffing position, head extended and neck flexed
Neutral in-line with a chin lift
Full extension with the shoulders padded
Supine with support under the shoulders and neck
questions.explanation: The sniffing position with head extended and neck flexed aligns the hypopharynx for the device to glide along the hard palate. The chin is gently pressed down before insertion begins.

questions.stem: In which direction does 8.14 direct the leading soft tip of the i-gel to be introduced into the mouth?
options: Toward the floor of the mouth
questions.explanation: The tip is introduced toward the hard palate, then glided downward and backward along it with continuous gentle pressure until definitive resistance is felt. Aiming elsewhere tends to fold the tip or catch the tongue.

questions.stem: Early resistance is met during i-gel insertion. What does 8.14 direct?
options: Perform a jaw thrust and insert with a deep rotation
Apply firm steady force until the resistance gives
Withdraw and select the next smaller size
Insert a finger to guide the device past the tongue
questions.explanation: Early resistance is managed with a jaw thrust and a deep rotation of the device. 8.14 forbids excessive force and notes it is not necessary to put fingers or thumbs into the patient's mouth during insertion.

questions.stem: How does 8.14 direct i-gel placement to be confirmed?
options: Waveform ETCO2 plus lung sounds in both fields and the epigastrium
Chest rise together with misting in the device
Aspiration of gastric contents through the gastric channel
questions.explanation: Confirmation requires waveform ETCO2 and auscultation of both lung fields and over the epigastrium. Epigastric sounds would indicate the device is seated incorrectly and ventilating the stomach.

questions.stem: In which i-gel sizes does 8.14 permit a #10 feeding tube to be passed down the gastric channel?
questions.explanation: The gastric channel will accept a #10 feeding tube only in size 1.5 and above; the size 1 neonatal device cannot take one. Decompressing the stomach reduces regurgitation risk around the cuff.

questions.stem: The taped securement technique described in 8.14 applies to which i-gel sizes?
questions.explanation: The two-piece nylon tape technique exists for the small devices — sizes 1 through 2.5 — because these tubes are too small for a commercial securement device. Adult sizes are secured with a commercial device.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed as an indication for inline nebulizer treatment in 8.15?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm, croup/epiglottitis/laryngospasm and hyperkalemia are the listed indications — the last because nebulized beta-agonist drives potassium intracellularly. 8.15 lists no contraindications.

questions.stem: In the adult/pediatric circuit diagram in 8.15, where does the inline nebulizer set-up sit?
options: Between the flow sensor and the vent tubing
Between the ETT and the ETCO2 adaptor
Between the ETCO2 adaptor and the flow sensor
Between the ETT and the flow sensor
questions.explanation: The circuit runs ETT > ETCO2 > flow sensor > inline neb set-up > vent tubing. Placing the nebulizer distal to the flow sensor would add dead space and corrupt the measured volumes.

questions.stem: What does 8.15 PEARLS warn will result from connecting the nebulizer between the flow sensor and the ETT?
options: Increased dead space and incorrect measurements
Delivery of the drug into the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: Putting the nebulizer distal to the flow sensor adds dead space between the sensor and the patient and makes the ventilator's measurements wrong. This is the single most common inline nebulizer set-up error.

questions.stem: On the Hamilton T1, for how long is the fixed nebulizer flow synchronized with the inspiratory phase of each breath?
questions.explanation: The Hamilton T1 runs the fixed nebulizer flow, using 100% O2, synchronized to inspiration for 30 minutes. Crews should expect the feature to stop on its own at that point rather than when the medication cup empties.

questions.stem: On the Hamilton T1, a pneumatic nebulizer connected to the nebulizer port is optimally specified for approximately what flow?
questions.explanation: The Hamilton T1 nebulizer port is specified for roughly 8 L/min, and the ventilator automatically compensates for the added volume so the set tidal volume is still delivered. The 6 L/min figure is the LTV/ReVel drive port flow.

questions.stem: When the nebulizer is activated on the LTV/ReVel ventilator, what nominal flow is delivered to the nebulizer drive port?
questions.explanation: The LTV/ReVel delivers a six L/min nominal flow of 100% oxygen to the nebulizer drive port, and reduces inspiratory limb flow to compensate at the patient wye. The 8 L/min figure belongs to the Hamilton T1.

questions.stem: How does 8.15 PEARLS direct an Aerogen nebulizer to be connected to the Hamilton T1?
options: Via the USB port on the side of the ventilator
Via the nebulizer port on the front panel
Via a T piece in the inspiratory limb
questions.explanation: The Aerogen is a vibrating-mesh device and takes its power from the USB port on the side of the Hamilton T1, not from the pneumatic nebulizer port used by jet nebulizers.

questions.stem: Which finding is listed as an indication for intracranial pressure monitoring in 8.16?
questions.explanation: Intraventricular bleeds, CT showing edema and/or shifts, confirmed head injury with GCS < 8 and posturing are the indications. 8.16 lists no contraindications.

questions.stem: Below which Glasgow Coma Scale score does 8.16 indicate ICP monitoring for a confirmed head injury?
questions.explanation: A confirmed head injury with a GCS below 8 is a listed indication, matching the conventional threshold at which a patient can no longer protect the airway or be followed by serial neuro exam.

questions.stem: Level with which anatomic landmark does 8.16 direct the ICP transducer to be placed and secured?
questions.explanation: The transducer is leveled to the foramen of Monro, on the same side the ventriculostomy catheter is inserted. A transducer leveled anywhere else produces an ICP reading that is wrong by the height difference.

questions.stem: With what does 8.16 direct the ICP transducer system to be primed?
options: Normal saline under a pressure bag
questions.explanation: Priming uses preservative-free normal saline under strict aseptic technique. 8.16 also directs that IV fluids must not be hung and a pressure bag must not be used — any pressurized infusion into a ventriculostomy is dangerous.

questions.stem: What is the first step in zeroing the ventriculostomy line, per 8.16?
options: Turn the stopcock open to air
Replace the cap and close the stopcock to air
questions.explanation: The stopcock is opened to air first, the waveform is observed to flatten, Zero is pressed, and only then is the cap replaced and the stopcock closed to air to begin transducing. Pressing Zero before opening to air zeroes against the patient's pressure.

questions.stem: When does 8.16 require the ventriculostomy drain to be closed during transport?
options: For all patient movements and altitude changes
Only when the ICP exceeds the ordered threshold
questions.explanation: The drain is closed for every patient movement and every altitude change. An open drain during a position or pressure change can siphon CSF uncontrollably.

questions.stem: What does 8.16 require each time the aircraft changes altitude with an ICP monitor in place?
options: Re-level the transducer to the foramen of Monro
Open the drain to equalize the pressure
questions.explanation: The transducer must be zeroed with each altitude change, because the reference pressure the system was zeroed against has moved. The drain stays closed throughout the altitude change.

questions.stem: What does 8.17 give as the indication for intranasal medication delivery?
options: IV access is not present or is undesirable
The patient is combative and cannot be restrained
The patient has a documented allergy to IM medications
Rapid onset is required during cardiac arrest
questions.explanation: The intranasal route exists for when IV access is absent or undesirable — the classic cases being a seizing patient, a combative overdose, or a child in whom a line would delay treatment.

questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates intranasal medication delivery under 8.17?
questions.explanation: Facial trauma, epistaxis, nasal congestion or discharge, and recent nasal cocaine use are the contraindications — each either blocks the mucosa or washes the drug away before it can be absorbed.

questions.stem: For a patient aged 10 years or older, what is the maximum intranasal volume 8.17 permits per nostril?
questions.explanation: Patients 10 years and older take no more than 1 mL per nostril. Larger volumes run out of the nose or down the pharynx instead of being absorbed across the nasal mucosa.

questions.stem: For a child under 10 years of age, what is the maximum intranasal volume 8.17 permits per nostril?
questions.explanation: Children under 10 take no more than 0.5 mL per nostril — half the adult limit. If the calculated volume exceeds this, the concentration must be increased rather than the volume.

questions.stem: How much extra medication does 8.17 direct to be drawn into the syringe to account for atomizer dead space?
questions.explanation: An extra 0.1 mL is drawn up because that volume remains in the mucosal atomizer device and never reaches the patient. Omitting it under-doses every intranasal administration.

questions.stem: Once the MAD is inserted into the nares, toward what does 8.17 direct the tip to be aimed?
options: The top of the ipsilateral ear
questions.explanation: Aiming at the top of the ear on the same side directs the spray onto the highly vascular superior turbinate region. Aiming at the septum sprays the drug onto a poorly absorbing surface.

questions.stem: When does 8.17 direct the plunger to be depressed during intranasal administration?
options: Slowly at the start of inhalation
Rapidly at the peak of inhalation
questions.explanation: The plunger is pushed rapidly, timed to exhalation but before the next breath in, so the atomized drug is deposited on the mucosa rather than inhaled into the lower airway.

questions.stem: What portion of the total intranasal dose does 8.17 direct to be given in each nare?
options: Half of the total dose in each nare
The entire dose in the larger nare
The entire dose divided over three doses
questions.explanation: Half the total dose goes in each nostril, doubling the mucosal surface area available for absorption and keeping the per-nostril volume within the 1 mL (or 0.5 mL pediatric) limit.

questions.stem: To improve the success of intranasal delivery, what does 8.17 direct regarding drug volume and concentration?
options: Minimize the volume and maximize the concentration
Maximize the volume and dilute the drug
Match the volume to the patient's weight
Use the standard IV concentration unchanged
questions.explanation: Absorption is limited by mucosal surface area, not by volume, so the smallest possible volume of the most concentrated preparation works best. Extra diluent simply runs out of the nose.

questions.stem: For which patient does 8.18 indicate intraosseous access?
options: A critical patient who needs immediate vascular access
A stable patient with historically difficult veins
A patient who needs a second line for a second infusion
A patient refusing peripheral IV attempts
questions.explanation: 8.18 lists only two indications: immediate vascular access in the critical patient, and cardiac arrest. Difficult venous access in a stable patient is not, by itself, a reason to drill.

questions.stem: Which finding at or near the intended insertion site contraindicates IO placement under 8.18?
options: A prosthetic implant in the opposite limb
A fracture of the intended insertion bone
An IO placed in the opposite limb 2 hours ago
A humeral site in a patient weighing 40 kg
questions.explanation: The three contraindications are a fracture of the intended insertion bone, a prosthetic implant at the insertion site, and recent IO access in the same limb. A prosthesis or a recent IO in the opposite limb does not bar the site you are using.

questions.stem: An IO was placed in a patient's left tibia and has since been removed. Within what period does 8.18 treat further IO access in that same limb as contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Recent (≤ 24 hours) IO access in the same limb is a contraindication, because extravasation from the earlier cortical breach makes infusate unreliable and risks compartment syndrome. The opposite limb remains available.

questions.stem: At what patient weight does 8.18 direct use of the EZ-IO 45 mm (yellow hub) needle for a humeral head insertion?
questions.explanation: The humeral head carries more overlying soft tissue than the tibial sites, so in patients ≥ 40 kg the 45 mm yellow hub needle is needed to reach the medullary space. Too short a needle seats in soft tissue and the infusion infiltrates.

questions.stem: With the IO needle tip resting on the bone before the trigger is squeezed, what confirms the needle is long enough?
options: The needle moves freely side to side
The stylet can be withdrawn without resistance
The hub sits flush against the skin
The 5-mm mark is visible above the skin
questions.explanation: The 5-mm mark is the most proximal mark to the hub; if it is still visible above the skin once the tip is on bone, there is enough needle left to cross the cortex. If it is not visible, 8.18 directs a longer needle and/or a different insertion site.

questions.stem: What tells you to immediately release the EZ-IO driver trigger during insertion?
options: A sudden pop or loss of resistance
Blood appears at the needle hub
questions.explanation: The sudden pop or loss of resistance means you have entered the medullary space; continuing to drive risks passing through the far cortex. Placement is then confirmed by flushing the cannula with saline.

questions.stem: 8.18 permits the distal femur as an adult IO insertion site only in patients up to what age?
questions.explanation: Adult sites are the proximal tibia, distal tibia and humeral head, with the distal femur allowed only if the patient is ≤ 21 years. Beyond that age the femoral marrow space is a poor target and the site is dropped.

questions.stem: What minimum weight does 8.18 set for the pediatric IO insertion sites?
questions.explanation: The pediatric sites — proximal tibia, distal tibia, humeral head and distal femur — apply to patients over 3 kg. Below that weight the bones are too small for the standard needle sets listed here.

questions.stem: How does 8.18 direct you to confirm IO placement once the cannula is seated and the stylet removed?
options: Aspirate bone marrow into the syringe
Flush the cannula rapidly with saline
Attach a pressure bag and watch the drip chamber
Check for a waveform on the monitor
questions.explanation: Placement is confirmed by flushing the cannula with saline, and a rapid flush is specifically necessary before infusing anything, because it displaces the bone marrow that would otherwise obstruct flow. Patency must be reconfirmed before any medication or fluid.

questions.stem: Flow through a correctly placed IO is inadequate for the volume you need. What does 8.18 direct, and which site generally flows best?
options: Replace the needle with a longer one; the proximal tibia generally flows best
Place a second IO in the same limb; the distal femur generally flows best
Use a pressure bag or IV pump; the humeral head generally flows best
Use a pressure bag or IV pump; the distal tibia generally flows best
questions.explanation: IO flow is pressure dependent, so 8.18 directs a pressure bag or IV pump when rates are inadequate, and notes the humeral head generally provides a higher flow rate than the other insertion sites.

questions.stem: Where is the adult proximal tibia IO insertion site in relation to the tibial tuberosity?
options: Approximately 2 cm lateral to the tuberosity
Approximately 3 cm proximal to the tuberosity
Approximately 2 cm medial to the tuberosity
questions.explanation: The adult proximal tibia site is about 2 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity, on the flat anterior surface. If the tuberosity cannot be palpated, the site is approximately 3 cm below the inferior border of the patella at that same level.

questions.stem: Where is the adult distal tibia IO insertion site located?
options: Approximately 3 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
Approximately 3 cm proximal to the lateral malleolus
Directly over the most prominent part of the malleolus
Approximately 1 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: The adult distal tibia site is roughly 3 cm proximal to the most prominent aspect of the medial malleolus, mid-line on the flat centre of the bone. The distal tibia usually has the least overlying tissue of any site.

questions.stem: Where is the pediatric distal femur IO insertion site located?
options: 1-2 cm distal to the inferior border of the patella, in the mid-line
1-2 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella, about 1 cm medial to mid-line
3 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella, about 1 cm lateral to mid-line
Directly over the superior border of the patella
questions.explanation: With the leg outstretched so the knee cannot bend, the pediatric distal femur site sits roughly 1-2 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella and about 1 cm medial to the mid-line. Letting the knee flex moves the landmark.

questions.stem: What must be achieved before a pediatric proximal humerus IO is attempted?
options: The deltoid insertion must be marked
The greater tubercle must be palpable
The arm must be abducted and externally rotated
questions.explanation: 8.18 states in red that you must be able to palpate the greater tubercle before insertion, to avoid errant placement. The arm is adducted and internally rotated — not abducted — to bring the tubercle up into the palm of your hand.

questions.stem: What is the adult initial dose of 2% lidocaine for IO pain management under 8.18?
questions.explanation: A conscious patient feels the infusate expanding the marrow cavity, so 8.18 gives 40 mg of 2% lidocaine before flushing. The weight-based figures are the lidocaine doses used for arrest and tachycardia, not for IO analgesia.

questions.stem: What is the pediatric initial dose of 2% lidocaine for IO pain management under 8.18?
questions.explanation: The pediatric initial dose is 0.5 mg/kg, capped at the adult dose of 40 mg. It is given by the same route and timing as the adult dose: slowly, directly into the catheter hub, before the flush.

questions.stem: What is the maximum initial dose of 2% lidocaine for pediatric IO pain management?
questions.explanation: The pediatric 0.5 mg/kg dose is capped at 40 mg, which is the adult dose, so a larger child never receives more than an adult would. The mg/kg ceilings belong to lidocaine's arrest and local-anaesthesia indications.

questions.stem: How is the initial dose of 2% lidocaine administered through an IO before the line is flushed?
options: Infuse over 60 seconds, then dwell 120 seconds
Infuse over 60 seconds, then flush immediately
Infuse over 120 seconds, then dwell 60 seconds
Infuse over 120 seconds, then flush immediately
questions.explanation: The lidocaine is infused slowly over 120 seconds and then allowed to dwell for 60 seconds so it can anaesthetise the marrow cavity before the normal saline flush drives it out. Flushing straight away wastes the dose and the flush still hurts.

questions.stem: The patient still reports pain after the initial IO lidocaine dose. What repeat dose does 8.18 direct, and over what time?
options: Half the initial dose, infused over 60 seconds
Half the initial dose, infused over 120 seconds
The full initial dose, infused over 60 seconds
The full initial dose, infused over 120 seconds
questions.explanation: If additional lidocaine is needed after reassessment, half of the initial dose is given over 60 seconds — half the dose and half the infusion time of the first dose. For an adult that is 20 mg.

questions.stem: Where is the lidocaine syringe attached when giving IO pain management under 8.18?
options: To the primed EZ-Connect extension set
Directly to the IO catheter hub, without the extension set
To a stopcock between the extension set and the flush
To the side port of a pressure-bagged fluid line
questions.explanation: The syringe goes straight onto the catheter hub with no extension set, so the whole dose reaches the marrow rather than sitting in the dead space of the tubing. The primed extension set is attached afterwards and the line is then flushed.

questions.stem: To what pressure does 8.19 direct you to inflate the pressure bag on an invasive monitoring set-up?
questions.explanation: The bag is inflated to 300 mmHg, above any arterial pressure the patient can generate, so the flush device delivers its continuous low-rate flush and the catheter does not clot or back up. An underinflated bag is a classic cause of an over-dampened trace.

questions.stem: Where is the transducer placed and secured for invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
options: At the mid-clavicular line, second intercostal space
questions.explanation: The transducer is levelled and secured at the phlebostatic axis, the reference point for the right atrium. If it drifts above or below that level during transport, every pressure it reports is offset.

questions.stem: What does 8.19 direct a crew to repeat with any change in altitude during transport?
options: Re-inflating the pressure bag to 300 mmHg
questions.explanation: Ambient pressure is the reference for the transducer, so a change in cabin altitude shifts the zero and every reading with it. 8.19 builds the re-zero into the zeroing step rather than leaving it to judgement.

questions.stem: During the zeroing sequence, what does 8.19 have you observe immediately after opening the stopcock to air?
questions.explanation: With the stopcock open to air, the square waveform test checks the dynamic response of the tubing and catheter before you press zero on the monitor. Comparing IBP with NIBP is the last step of the procedure, after the stopcock is returned.

questions.stem: The sending facility's transducer is not compatible with LFN equipment. What does 8.19 direct?
options: Use the existing line and zero it to the LFN monitor
Switch the line out and set up an LFN transducer
Monitor with NIBP alone for the transport
questions.explanation: 8.19 permits using an existing line only when its transducer is compatible with LFN equipment; otherwise the line must be switched out and primed from step 3. An incompatible transducer cannot be reliably zeroed or read by the LFN monitor.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform has become flat and over-dampened. Which check does 8.19 direct?
options: Flush the catheter with a heparin syringe
Confirm no white caps remain in the set-up
Reposition the patient's arm and re-measure
questions.explanation: The over-dampened checklist is mechanical: air or kinks, pressure bag inflation, white caps left in place of dead-end caps, tubing disconnected from the patient, transducer position and waveform scale. A flat trace is far more often a set-up fault than a true loss of pressure.

questions.stem: Which port should be used to give medications to a patient with a pulmonary artery catheter?
options: Any open stopcock on the transducer
questions.explanation: 8.19 prohibits infusing medications through the distal PA port and directs that the right ventricular port be used; it may be capped and flushed. Drug delivered into the pulmonary artery bypasses mixing and the distal port is the pressure-monitoring lumen.

questions.stem: What does 8.19 say about obtaining a PCWP during transport of a patient with a pulmonary artery catheter?
options: There is no indication to wedge; document a PCWP before departure if available
Wedge only with medical control approval
Wedge the catheter once per hour and document the value
Wedge only if the distal waveform is dampened
questions.explanation: There is no transport indication for a PCWP, so the catheter should not be wedged — wedging risks pulmonary artery rupture and infarction. Any PCWP available from the sending unit is simply documented before departure.

questions.stem: Monitoring shows a PCWP tracing even though the wedge balloon is deflated. What does 8.19 direct?
options: Flush the distal port and continue monitoring
Withdraw the catheter until the PA waveform returns
Inflate and deflate the balloon to reposition the tip
questions.explanation: A spontaneous wedge means the catheter tip has migrated distally and the vessel is occluded, which risks infarction. 8.19 does not authorise crews to reposition the catheter; it directs contacting medical control.

questions.stem: Which patient meets the indication for a King airway under 8.20?
options: Unconscious with respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex
Responsive with an intact gag reflex
questions.explanation: The single indication is an unconscious patient with respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex. Caustic ingestion, known esophageal disease and a retained gag reflex are the three listed contraindications.

questions.stem: Which history contraindicates placing a King airway under 8.20?
questions.explanation: Caustic ingestion and known esophageal disease are contraindications because the distal cuff seats in an esophagus that may already be injured or friable. Suspected spinal injury is not a bar — the guideline simply directs maintaining spinal motion restriction instead of the sniffing position.

questions.stem: What determines which size KING LT(S)-D is selected?
options: The width of the mouth opening
The distance from incisors to angle of the jaw
questions.explanation: Sizing is by weight or height, matching the manufacturer's colour-coded scheme. An undersized tube will not seal and an oversized one will not seat to the teeth.

questions.stem: How is the KING LT(S)-D introduced into the mouth, and when is it rotated?
options: Midline at 90°, rotated to the corner of the mouth once past the teeth
Into the corner of the mouth at 90°, rotated back to midline as the tip passes under the tongue
Midline along the hard palate, with no rotation
Into the corner of the mouth inverted, rotated 180° at the oropharynx
questions.explanation: The tube goes in at the corner of the mouth at a 90° angle and is rotated back to midline as the tip passes under the tongue, which sweeps the tongue out of the way and keeps the tip off the posterior pharyngeal wall.

questions.stem: How far is the KING LT(S)-D inserted?
options: Until resistance is met at the upper esophageal sphincter
To a depth of three times the tube's internal diameter
Until the flange of the connector aligns with the teeth
Until the proximal cuff is level with the lips
questions.explanation: The tube is advanced until the flange of the connector lines up with the teeth, and 8.20 specifically warns not to force insertion. Inflating the cuffs then lifts the device slightly as it seats.

questions.stem: What ETCO2 finding does 8.20 describe as indicating appropriate ventilation through a King airway?
options: A rising value over three breaths
A value within 2-5 of the PCO2
questions.explanation: ETCO2 must be attached to confirm placement and continuous monitoring maintained; a normal four-phase waveform is the sign that ventilation is reaching the lungs. Chest rise and bilateral breath sounds are assessed alongside it.

questions.stem: Ventilation cannot be accomplished through a newly placed King airway. What is the first corrective step in 8.20?
options: Without deflating the cuff, pull back slightly and re-attempt ventilation
Add air to the cuffs and apply firmer downward pressure
Deflate the cuffs and advance the tube further
Withdraw the device completely and ventilate with a BVM
questions.explanation: The usual fault is the distal tip sitting too deep, so the first move is to pull back slightly with the cuffs still inflated and re-attempt. Only if that fails to seat the device is the cuff deflated and the tube slowly withdrawn and reassessed.

questions.stem: What does 8.20 direct you to do with the inflation syringe after the cuffs are inflated?
options: Leave it attached to the inflation port
Place it to the right of the patient's head
Tape it to the tube at the level of the teeth
Discard it in the sharps container
questions.explanation: The syringe is not discarded; it is kept to the right of the patient's head so the cuffs can be deflated instantly if the device has to be repositioned or removed. Suction must also be available whenever the device is removed.

questions.stem: For which airways does 8.21 make continuous ETCO2 monitoring mandatory?
options: Endotracheal tubes and surgical airways only
Any airway when the patient is being transported by air
All advanced airways, including ETT, SGA and surgical cricothyrotomy
questions.explanation: Continuous ETCO2 is mandatory for every patient with an advanced airway — ETT, supraglottic airway or surgical cricothyrotomy — for the duration of transport. Its purpose is to catch unrecognised extubation and esophageal intubation.

questions.stem: There is no consistent ETCO2 waveform on an intubated patient. What does 8.21 direct?
options: Replace the ETCO2 sensor and continue ventilating
Auscultate the chest and epigastrium and continue if breath sounds are present
Increase the ventilation rate and reassess in one minute
Remove the ETT and ventilate by other means, or directly visualise the tube through the cords
questions.explanation: Without a consistent waveform the tube must be assumed misplaced: either remove it and ventilate by BVM, SGA or another intubation attempt, or prove placement by direct visualisation of the tube through the vocal cords. Breath sounds alone are not accepted as the substitute.

questions.stem: Secretions and blood are interfering with ETCO2 measurement on an intubated patient. Which two options does 8.21 give?
options: Remove the tube and provide effective BVM, or directly visualise the tube witnessed by another provider
Switch to colorimetric ETCO2, or document the absence of a waveform
Suction and accept the reading, or increase the ventilation rate
Remove the tube and place an SGA, or extubate and use high-flow oxygen
questions.explanation: When operational factors make the capnogram unreadable there are exactly two sanctioned options: remove the tube and ventilate effectively with a BVM, or have the tube's position directly visualised and witnessed by another LFN or EMS provider, using the CMAC's recording feature.

questions.stem: Where does 8.21 direct an HMEF to be placed when secretions, blood or vomit are fouling the capnography line?
options: Immediately proximal to the oxygen source
Between the ETT/SGA and the ETCO2 sensor
Between the ETCO2 sensor and the BVM
On the expiratory limb of the ventilator circuit
questions.explanation: The HMEF sits between the airway device and the ETCO2 sensor, so it traps secretions before they reach the sensor. It is placed after effective airway suctioning, not instead of it.

questions.stem: What does 8.21 suggest considering to facilitate ventilation in a patient with an advanced airway?
options: A PEEP valve on the BVM
A second ETCO2 sensor on the expiratory limb
An OG tube to decompress the stomach
A nasopharyngeal airway alongside the ETT
questions.explanation: Gastric distension from pre-intubation bagging splints the diaphragm and worsens compliance, so 8.21 directs considering an OG tube to decompress the stomach and make ventilation easier.

questions.stem: How does 8.22 direct a STEMI or other critical patient who has not arrested to be transported?
options: On the AutoPulse running in continuous mode
On the AutoPulse in place with the LifeBand left open
Without a mechanical CPR device, which is applied only if arrest occurs
On the AutoPulse in place but powered OFF
questions.explanation: Critical non-arrest patients are preferentially transported with the AutoPulse already in place but powered off, so that if they decompensate there is no delay in starting compressions. Applying the device mid-arrest in a moving aircraft is the thing this avoids.

questions.stem: Where is the LUCAS suction cup positioned on the chest?
options: Over the lower half of the sternum, immediately above the xiphoid
At the inter-nipple line, centred on the left sternal border
Over the upper half of the sternum, below the manubrium
questions.explanation: The suction cup sits over the lower half of the sternum, immediately above the xiphoid. Too low compresses the xiphoid and abdominal organs; too high wastes force on the manubrium and generates no flow.

questions.stem: After pressing the LUCAS suction cup to the chest, what is done before compressions are started?
options: Draw a marker circle around the suction cup
Select PAUSE to lock the start position
Select CONTINUE to allow automatic sizing
questions.explanation: PAUSE locks the LUCAS start position at the depth you have set, which is what makes the compressions reproducible; compressions are then begun in Continuous or 30:2 per protocol. The marker circle and stabilization strap come afterwards.

questions.stem: When does 8.22 direct the LUCAS back plate to be slid beneath the patient, and to what level?
options: Once the patient is on the stretcher, to the level of the shoulders
Before manual CPR begins, to the level of the xiphoid
During the next planned rhythm check, to just below the axillae
After the first defibrillation, to the level of the iliac crests
questions.explanation: The back plate goes in during a rhythm check that was going to happen anyway, positioned below the axillae, so the only interruption in compressions is one that was already planned. Manual CPR continues the whole time the device is being prepared.

questions.stem: What anatomic landmark is aligned with the AutoPulse platform reference marks?
questions.explanation: The patient is transferred onto the platform with the axillae lined up to the reference marks and the torso centred, which puts the LifeBand across the correct part of the chest. A patient positioned too high or low on the platform compresses the wrong level.

questions.stem: Once the AutoPulse LifeBand is closed across the chest, which buttons are pressed and in what order?
questions.explanation: CONTINUE lets the device perform its automatic sizing and calibration to the patient's chest, and only then does START begin compressions. Pressing START first would compress against an uncalibrated band.

questions.stem: Which AutoPulse indicator confirms the device is set to deliver continuous compressions?
options: The LifeBand tension indicator is green
The infinity sign button is lighted
The battery indicator shows three bars
questions.explanation: 8.22 states the infinity sign button should be lighted to provide continuous compressions. If it is not, the device is cycling 30:2 rather than compressing continuously.

questions.stem: A mechanical CPR device alarms in flight and cannot be corrected immediately. What does 8.22 direct?
options: Cycle the power and allow the self-test to complete
Continue the device and troubleshoot at the receiving facility
Pause compressions until the alarm is cleared
questions.explanation: A malfunctioning device is removed from the equation and manual CPR resumes immediately — on the AutoPulse that means taking the patient off the device. Troubleshooting never takes priority over perfusion.

questions.stem: Which event does 8.22 accept as a reason to pause the mechanical CPR device during transport?
options: Repositioning the patient on the stretcher
